analysis.one_liner: Speeds up credit card reforms already passed and freezes rate and fee increases on existing balances.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 331-92 with heavy bipartisan support, but the Senate never voted, and the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Credit CARD Act of 2009 set its new credit card rules to take effect on February 22, 2010. Until then, the old rules still applied, so issuers could keep changing rates, fees, and terms on money customers had already borrowed. This bill would have made the CARD Act's main protections effective the day the president signed it and frozen interest rates, fees, and finance charges on existing balances until February 22, 2010. It passed the House 331-92 but the Senate never brought it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders carrying balances. The freeze would have stopped rate, fee, and finance-charge increases on money they had already borrowed through the 2009 holiday season. Protections against oversized penalty fees and rules protecting young consumers would have started immediately instead of in February, and someone who paid off a card within 45 days of a new-fee notice could not have their credit score damaged for it. Cardholders with multiple interest rates had to wait until February 2010 for the rule sending payments above the minimum to the highest-rate balance first.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the CARD Act's titles on consumer protection, enhanced consumer disclosures, and protections for young consumers effective on the date of enactment instead of February 22, 2010, though issuers with fewer than two million cards in circulation keep the original date.

Prohibits any creditor, from enactment until February 22, 2010, from raising the annual percentage rate, fee, or finance charge on an outstanding credit card balance or changing the terms for repaying it, except as the CARD Act itself allows.
Moves up to enactment the effective date of the requirement that penalty fees — late fees, over-limit fees, and similar charges — be reasonable and proportional to the violation.

Bars creditors and consumer reporting agencies from using the payoff or closure of a card account to hurt a consumer's credit score when the consumer pays off the balance within 45 days of notice of a new fee.
Clarifies that nothing in the 45-day notice rule stops a creditor from cutting a rate, reducing or eliminating a fee, or improving terms for the consumer immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Large credit card issuers — chiefly big banks — would have lost months of elevated revenue from rate and fee increases on existing balances and faced the cost of reprogramming their systems on an accelerated schedule before the Federal Reserve's final implementing rules were finished. Issuers with fewer than two million cards were exempted from the accelerated deadlines and kept the original timeline.

drawbacks.text: In exchange for the rate freeze, the bill delays until February 22, 2010 the CARD Act rule requiring payments above the minimum to go first to the balance with the highest interest rate, so cardholders juggling several rates did not get that benefit early.

Issuers with fewer than two million credit cards in circulation keep the original effective dates for most provisions, creating a two-track system in which their customers wait for the same protections.

The bill accelerates deadlines while the Federal Reserve's final implementing rules are still unwritten; an amendment requiring the Fed to certify the schedule was feasible by December 1, 2009 — with the provisions void otherwise — was rejected 171-253.
The freeze covers outstanding balances only and leaves untouched the rate-increase exceptions the CARD Act itself allows, such as increases tied to a moving index.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households carrying credit card debt into the 2009 holiday season, the freeze was the substance: it would have stopped increases on balances they had already rung up. The trade-offs were real but modest — the highest-rate-first payment rule waited until February, small issuers got extra time, and big issuers had to comply quickly without final Fed rules, which was the core objection raised on the House floor. The larger weakness was political: none of it mattered, because the Senate never acted.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House 331-92, but the Senate referred it to its Banking Committee, which never reported it out, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee held a hearing on October 8, 2009, marked the bill up on October 22, and reported it amended by voice vote on October 26.

On November 4, 2009, the House rejected a motion to recommit that would have required the Federal Reserve to certify the accelerated schedule was feasible by December 1, 2009, or sections 2 and 3 would have no effect, by a vote of 171-253.
The House passed the bill 331-92 the same day: Democrats favored it 248-1, while Republicans split 83 for and 91 against.

The Senate received the bill on November 5, 2009, referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee on December 23, 2009, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
Under the law as written, the CARD Act's protections took effect on the original schedule, February 22, 2010, with no freeze on rate increases in the months before.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large credit card issuers. They kept the original 2010 timeline and remained free, under the old rules, to raise rates and fees on existing balances for the three extra months the bill would have eliminated.

for.name: Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to move up the CARD Act's effective dates and added a freeze on rate and fee increases on existing balances.

for.name: Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill through committee — hearing on October 8, markup and voice-vote report on October 22-26 — and managed it on the House floor.

for.name: 248 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, 248 to 1.

against.name: Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 23, 2009; the committee never reported it out, and no vote ever occurred.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote at any point in the more than a year between House passage and the end of the Congress.

against.name: Banking industry trade groups
against.role: Credit card issuers and bank lobbies
against.what_they_did: Urged Congress to keep the CARD Act's original February 2010 timeline, arguing issuers needed the lead time to reprogram systems and had already repriced accounts in reliance on it.

against.name: Mike Castle
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions requiring the Federal Reserve to certify by December 1, 2009 that the accelerated implementation was feasible, with the core provisions void otherwise; the motion failed 171-253.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was 331-92: Democrats were nearly unanimous at 248-1 in favor, while Republicans split roughly down the middle, 83 yes to 91 no.

industries.note: The bill would have cut off three months early the window in which issuers could raise rates and fees on money cardholders had already borrowed, and frozen such increases until February 22, 2010. That directly reduced the revenue issuers collect from existing balances, which is why the freeze was the provision customers stood to feel most.

industries.industry: Small banks and credit unions that issue cards
industries.note: Issuers with fewer than two million cards in circulation were carved out of the accelerated dates and kept the original 2010 schedule, sparing them rapid compliance costs. The freeze on raising rates on existing balances applied to them all the same.

The bill barred both creditors and credit bureaus from using a card payoff or closure to lower a consumer's credit score when the consumer pays off within 45 days of a new-fee notice, removing one way account data feeds into scoring.
